item.title: AI stocks rebound on Wall Street but Treasury yields could pour cold water on the recovery
item.description:
It didn't take long for US equities to seek out a bit of a breather, with the bounce yesterday looking fairly decent after tech stocks were trounced in the week before. The Nasdaq climbed by 1.1% on Monday, recovering some ground after last week's heavy selloff, while the S&P 500 added 0.4%.

Sure, it's a decent start to the week. However, let's not forget how poorly things played out last week for tech stocks even as Treasury yields fell. That definitely left investors questioning whether the struggling market breadth and momentum is finally catching up or whether the enormous spending behind the AI boom is beginning to fail to justify lofty valuations.

In any case, I would argue that the bond market will still have a big say in how all of this plays out.

10-year Treasury yields are still keeping above 5% and nudged a little higher overnight to 5.12%. That is hardly a comfortable backdrop for tech stocks as the "higher for longer" environment means investors will likely have to get used to elevated interest rates sticking around. In turn, that will make future earnings less valuable today while raising financing costs.

And even if Treasury yields were to retreat a little as we saw last week, borrowing costs across the economy are still painfully high. That makes it harder to justify aggressive spending, particularly for companies relying heavily on debt.

As such, don't discount the potential impact from the bond market in trading this week even though things have been a bit quieter since the second half of last week. It will not take much to stoke the flames and reignite the jitters among broader markets.

Until the bond market settles down, I'd be careful about taking this little rebound for the start of another sustained rally in AI stocks.

Besides that, do keep a watchful eye on key tech earnings this week. In particular, I'd be watching Meta but not just for the earnings numbers and financial results. What I'll be keeping a close eye on is whether all that AI spending is starting to deliver meaningful returns.

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.

item.title: How to trade gold today before Netflix reports tonight
item.description:
Gold futures outlook today: Why buying low and selling high may beat chasing breakouts

Gold futures traders may currently find more attractive opportunities by buying weakness and selling strength than by chasing the next breakout. The reason is relatively simple: COMEX gold futures (GC) have repeatedly moved within a broader trading range of $4,091 to $4,250, without establishing a sustained directional move beyond either boundary.

That does not mean gold cannot break out tomorrow, or even today. It means traders should first recognize the market environment they are dealing with and adjust their expectations accordingly.

Based on the four-hour analysis entering October 20, 2026, the evidence still favors a predominantly sideways market, with a modest bearish tilt in the shorter-term price action.

Gold futures technical analysis: The $4,091-$4,250 range matters

One of the more useful observations from the recent gold futures price action is how frequently the market has rejected attempts to move beyond its established boundaries.

Consider the following historical examples:

  • On September 30, gold briefly traded above $4,250, reaching approximately $4,251, before closing the four-hour period near $4,209.

  • On October 2, another attempt reached approximately $4,259, but the four-hour close was around $4,221.

  • On October 7, gold tested the $4,091 area and subsequently recovered.

  • On October 14, another decline toward approximately $4,095 was followed by a meaningful rebound.

Across the 96 reviewed four-hour observations from September 28 through October 19, closing prices remained between approximately $4,106 and $4,236.

That is an important distinction. Gold has certainly experienced meaningful short-term rallies and selloffs, but those movements have repeatedly failed to develop into sustained breakouts from the broader range.

The reaction after testing a price boundary can be more informative than the initial attempt to break it.

When price moves above resistance but quickly returns below it, traders have evidence that the breakout has not yet attracted enough sustained buying to establish a new trading regime.

The opposite applies at support. A brief move toward or below an established floor does not necessarily indicate that a major bearish trend has begun.

In this environment, the broader range remains a useful reference for assessing where buyers and sellers may become more active.

Two important gold trading ranges, and why they are different

The current analysis identifies two ranges that serve different purposes.

1. The broader trading range: $4,091-$4,250

This is the larger market structure.

The lower region around $4,091-$4,120 may become interesting for traders looking for a bullish reversal, particularly if price approaches that area and buyers begin demonstrating renewed strength.

The upper region around $4,215-$4,250 may become interesting for traders looking for a bearish reversal, especially if a rally begins to lose momentum or a breakout attempt fails.

Neither area is an automatic buy or sell instruction. Price behavior near these boundaries remains essential.

2. The tighter value area: $4,158-$4,215

Within the larger trading range, historical volume concentration identifies a narrower area where a substantial portion of trading activity has occurred.

Its principal reference levels are:

$4,215: Value Area High (VAH)

The upper edge of the area containing concentrated trading activity. It can act as a reference when evaluating whether price is moving toward the upper portion of the current balance.

$4,185: Point of Control (POC)

The price at which the greatest volume was traded over the selected analysis period. In a balanced market, it can become a useful reference for potential price rotation.

$4,158: Value Area Low (VAL)

The lower edge of the concentrated trading area. A successful defense of this region could support a recovery toward the interior of the value area.

Importantly, the point of control is not a guaranteed magnet. Gold can move away from it and establish a new area of trading activity.

An easy way to remember the distinction is this:

The broader range defines the battlefield. The tighter value area helps identify where much of the trading business has been conducted within it.

Gold price outlook for October 20: What traders can watch

In the latest supplied market snapshot entering October 20, gold was trading around $4,163, after recovering from an October 19 intraday low near $4,134.50.

That places gold near the lower boundary of its tighter value area, but still some distance above the broader $4,091 support region.

Although the shorter-term structure has weakened, that weakness has not established a breakdown from the wider trading range.

Several scenarios deserve consideration.

Scenario 1: Buyers defend $4,158

If gold stabilizes and sustains trading above approximately $4,158, the next area to monitor is around $4,175, followed by the $4,185 point of control.

This would represent a possible recovery within the existing trading range rather than necessarily the beginning of a sustained bullish trend.

For traders entering near the lower value-area boundary, a recovery toward the point of control could offer an opportunity to reassess the position or consider partial profit-taking.

However, a failed attempt to hold $4,158 would weaken this immediate recovery scenario.

Scenario 2: Gold declines toward $4,091-$4,120

If gold loses $4,158 and subsequently breaks below the recent $4,134-$4,140 support region, attention could turn toward the lower boundary of the broader trading range.

This is where recognizing the market regime becomes particularly valuable.

A trader focused exclusively on the latest bearish momentum might interpret the decline as an invitation to pursue further selling.

But a trader who recognizes the broader range might instead begin watching for signs of stabilization, failed selling pressure or a recovery from the established support region.

Neither interpretation guarantees a profitable trade.

The key is whether price confirms continued weakness or begins to reject the lower prices.

Scenario 3: Gold rallies toward $4,215-$4,250

A recovery above $4,185 could bring the upper value-area boundary near $4,215 back into focus.

If gold continues toward the $4,215-$4,250 region, traders may want to become increasingly selective about pursuing additional upside.

Under the current range-bound interpretation, this upper region is where potential bearish reversals deserve attention.

A failed attempt to hold above resistance could reinforce the existing sideways structure.

Conversely, sustained buying beyond $4,250 would provide evidence that the market may be transitioning into a more bullish environment.

An important trading lesson: Identify the market regime before choosing the strategy

Markets generally do not move in one direction indefinitely.

Sometimes they establish persistent trends. At other times, they consolidate, repeatedly moving between recognizable areas of support and resistance.

The reasons can vary.

Market participants might be waiting for economic releases, central-bank decisions, geopolitical developments or other significant news. Sometimes buyers and sellers are simply reaching a temporary balance.

And occasionally, the explanation is not immediately obvious.

But here is a useful trading lesson: You do not necessarily need to know why the market is moving sideways before recognizing that it is moving sideways.

Consider a hypothetical trader watching gold decline sharply from $4,200 toward $4,160.

On a shorter-term chart, the decline may appear aggressively bearish. Sellers may be dominating the latest price action, and several short-term signals may support the bearish interpretation.

Yet on the broader four-hour structure, gold could simply be completing another rotation toward the lower half of its established range.

Both observations can be correct.

The problem arises when traders confuse a short-term directional move with a change in the broader market environment.

This is one reason breakout strategies can become frustrating during prolonged consolidation.

A market may repeatedly appear ready to begin a substantial directional move, only to reverse and return toward the middle of its trading range.

In those conditions, traders who adapt their strategies to the observed environment may find more appropriate setups than those who repeatedly anticipate the next major breakout.

A good directional analysis is not automatically a good trading opportunity. The location of the potential trade within the prevailing market structure also matters.

When would the sideways gold market interpretation change?

The current range-bound assessment is conditional, not permanent.

A meaningful change would involve gold establishing sustained acceptance outside the broader $4,091-$4,250 range.

A bullish transition above $4,250

A four-hour close above $4,250, followed by continued buying or a successful retest of the former resistance region, would strengthen the argument that gold is leaving its sideways trading environment.

A bearish transition below $4,091

A sustained move below $4,091, accompanied by follow-through or a failed attempt to reclaim the broken support, would weaken the range-trading thesis and favor reassessing downside risks.

In either case, one brief price excursion beyond the boundary would be less convincing than evidence that the market can actually remain outside the previous range.

The important concept is acceptance: price holding beyond a previous boundary rather than briefly crossing it.

Of course, waiting for confirmation does not eliminate false breakouts. It simply provides an additional way to distinguish a potential regime change from another temporary excursion.

Managing risk when trading a sideways gold market

Range trading can offer attractive opportunities, but it also presents meaningful risks.

A particularly dangerous assumption is that a previously respected support or resistance level must continue working indefinitely.

It does not.

Eventually, some trading ranges end with a sustained directional move.

That is why traders considering entries near the range boundaries should establish their invalidation conditions and position sizes in advance.

Partial profit-taking can also be useful. For example, a trader entering a long position near a defended lower boundary may choose to reduce exposure as price approaches an important reference such as the $4,185 point of control.

Following an initial profitable exit, traders may consider reducing the remaining risk or moving a stop toward their entry price, depending on their trading plan.

However, moving a stop to entry does not guarantee a cost-free outcome because commissions, spreads and slippage still matter.

Another practical consideration is that a potential opportunity near a range boundary does not justify entering without evidence that the expected reversal is developing.

Patience is part of the strategy.

Final takeaway for gold traders

The most useful conclusion from the current gold futures analysis is not a prediction that gold will rise or fall next.

It is that the available price evidence continues to favor a range-bound environment, even though short-term bearish pressure has recently increased.

Within that environment, the $4,091-$4,250 broader range and the $4,158-$4,215 value area provide practical reference points for evaluating potential trades.

Gold traders do not necessarily need to discover why the market is consolidating. They need to recognize that it is consolidating, understand where the meaningful boundaries are and adjust their expectations.

Until gold demonstrates that a new directional regime has begun, buying weakness and selling strength near established boundaries may make more sense than chasing every potential breakout.

This analysis is based on historical four-hour gold futures observations through October 19, 2026, and a market snapshot entering October 20. Levels refer to the continuous COMEX gold futures series, not necessarily another gold instrument or contract. Educational market analysis only, not personalized investment advice. Trading futures involves substantial risk of loss.

The energy-driven macro narrative is heavily dictating cross-asset order flow this week.

As Eamonn Sheridan at investingLive.com pointed out, Brent crude is currently pricing in a $25 war risk premium, prompting Goldman Sachs to revise its December target to the $90 level as traders weigh the threat of supply curtailment against recovering Gulf exports.

This persistent strength in energy is creating a challenging microstructure for precious metals. According to the latest breakdown by Adam Button at investingLive.com, CIBC has significantly downgraded its near-term gold outlook to $4,500 for Q4, citing the stronger US dollar and tighter Fed policy expectations generated by these very inflation shocks.

  • The PBOC set its USD/CNY reference rate at the strongest level for the yuan since 2 February 2023.

  • Bank research dominated a light news day, with Goldman Sachs, BlackRock, Morgan Stanley and Citi weighing in on higher bond yields and their role in portfolios.

Asian markets drifted lower on Tuesday in a session light on fresh news, as China kept its benchmark lending rates on hold and guided the yuan to its strongest official fixing in more than three and a half years.

China left its one-year loan prime rate at 3.0% and the five-year rate at 3.5%, extending the hold to 17 months. The decision was widely expected after stronger-than-forecast third-quarter growth reduced pressure for easing. The rates have taken a back seat as policy tools, with the central bank’s seven-day reverse repo rate serving as its main policy signal, though the LPR remains the benchmark for most loans and mortgages.

The bigger policy story came from China’s money markets. The People’s Bank of China said it will conduct daily overnight reverse repo operations from 21 October to 2 November, capped at 1 trillion yuan a day, a day after Governor Pan Gongsheng said the central bank would study making the overnight rate its main policy rate. The rate attached to the operations has not yet been confirmed and will be closely watched for signs of whether a lower policy anchor is coming.

The PBOC also set its daily yuan reference rate at the strongest level for the Chinese currency since 2 February 2023, signalling comfort with a firmer yuan. MUFG said this week that improving Chinese activity offers a more supportive backdrop for the currency, though it cautioned that weak household demand and a deepening property slump could limit the gains.

Regional stocks were softer. Hong Kong’s Hang Seng fell about 1%, the Shanghai Composite eased around 0.5% and Japan’s Nikkei slipped about 0.6%, following last week’s tech-led selling on Wall Street.

Oil prices edged higher despite no new developments in the Middle East, with WTI around $99 a barrel and Brent near $110. Goldman Sachs said last week that Brent carries a risk premium of nearly $25 a barrel above fair value tied to the Iran war, and data showed the US Strategic Petroleum Reserve has fallen to its lowest level since 1982. Gold dipped toward $4,125 an ounce before recovering to around $4,140, with Goldman estimating central banks bought 79 tonnes in August and describing official demand as a structural support.

Bank research filled much of the gap left by the light news calendar, with a common theme of higher yields forcing harder choices. Goldman Sachs said intensifying competition for capital from government borrowing and AI investment has made higher yields the global norm. BlackRock said France’s bond sell-off shows why investors must be selective, and upgraded US Treasuries. Morgan Stanley Investment Management argued yields are rising for the right reasons, reflecting strong growth. Citi Australia Chief Executive Mark Woodruff took a more cautious line on bonds, telling reporters in Sydney that rising supply, sticky inflation and higher neutral rates are making Treasuries a weaker hedge for stocks.

In technology, UBS said last week’s sell-off in specialist AI cloud providers does not derail the broader AI investment cycle, and Morgan Stanley named Amazon a top pick on faster cloud growth.

Geopolitics remained in focus after US officials said Washington has not approved the transfer of Patriot interceptor missiles to Ukraine, the Washington Post reported, amid a dispute over Ukrainian strikes on Russian energy infrastructure.

Looking ahead, attention turns to UK inflation data and Moody’s review of France’s credit rating, followed next week by central bank decisions from the Bank of Canada, where Scotiabank expects a rate hike, and the Bank of Japan, where Daiwa sees a hold but a shift toward keeping inflation anchored at 2%.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Daiwa: BOJ shifts focus from reaching 2% inflation to keeping it there, wages hold the key
item.description:
Daiwa’s reading points to a BOJ that is not in a hurry but has not finished hiking, which keeps the yen supported on any sign that wage growth is becoming entrenched. A hold at the 29-30 October meeting, paired with an upgraded inflation assessment, would keep a December hike in play and could lift short-dated Japanese government bond yields. Oil is a key swing factor: Daiwa notes import prices have started rising again on higher crude, and any further jump in oil linked to the Iran war would add to the risk of inflation overshooting, strengthening the case for faster tightening. For Japanese equities, gradual hikes alongside solid capital spending are unlikely to derail the market, though a faster pace would test valuations. Long-dated JGBs, where yields have already risen above 3%, remain sensitive to any shift in the BOJ’s tone.

-

After decades of trying to get inflation up to 2%, the Bank of Japan’s new problem is making sure it stays there, and Daiwa says the answer will be found in next spring’s pay packets.

Summary:

  • Daiwa says the BOJ is shifting from trying to lift underlying inflation to 2% to keeping it stable around that level.
  • Governor Kazuo Ueda said on 16 October that underlying inflation is broadly close to 2% and that a further rise from here cannot be tolerated.
  • The BOJ is expected to hold its 1.25% policy rate on 29-30 October but may upgrade its inflation assessment, with a December hike reportedly not ruled out.
  • Japan’s largest union group, Rengo, is considering seeking pay rises of 5% or more in 2027 for a fourth straight year, with an aim of 6%.
  • Daiwa says the durability and breadth of wage gains, including at smaller firms, will be key to the timing of future hikes.
  • Import prices have started rising again on higher crude oil, adding to inflation risks.

The Bank of Japan is entering a new phase in which its goal is no longer to lift inflation to 2% but to keep it there, according to Daiwa Securities, which says the durability of wage growth will be key to the timing of further rate increases.

At a press conference on 16 October, Governor Kazuo Ueda said underlying inflation was broadly close to 2% and that a further rise from that level could not be tolerated. He indicated that while the central bank had previously been willing to let underlying inflation climb toward its target, keeping it firmly anchored around 2% would now be a central policy objective. Daiwa said the remarks confirm a shift it had previously identified, from a policy of reaching 2% to one of stabilising inflation at that level.

Ueda said the policy board would discuss in depth whether underlying inflation has reached 2% at its meeting on 29 and 30 October. Citing reports, Daiwa said the BOJ is likely to leave its policy rate at 1.25% at that meeting but may upgrade its assessment of underlying inflation to broadly around 2%. That would not be treated as an immediate achievement of the price target, and the central bank is expected to keep raising rates while financial conditions remain accommodative, with a December hike reportedly not ruled out.

Daiwa said there is no need to accelerate the pace of rate increases, given that consumer spending remains weak even as business investment holds up. Core machinery orders rose 5.2% in August, pointing to resilient capital spending, including in AI-related sectors. Equally, it argued that inflation pressures have not clearly faded. Corporate goods prices rose 6.8% from a year earlier in September, easing from 7.6% in August but still elevated, while import prices have begun rising again on the back of higher crude oil prices.

The bank sees next year’s spring wage negotiations as the key test of whether inflation has become established. Rengo, Japan’s largest trade union federation, is reportedly considering calling for pay rises of 5% or more in 2027, the fourth straight year at that level, with a higher target of 6% or more for smaller firms and an aim of around 6% overall. This year’s negotiations delivered rises of about 5%, though gains at smaller companies were lower at around 4.7%.

Daiwa said what matters is not just the headline figure but whether strong pay rises become a lasting norm and spread from large companies to smaller ones. More detail will emerge over the coming months, including Rengo’s basic plan in October and the business lobby Keidanren’s position in November, giving the BOJ a clearer read by its December meeting.

For now, Daiwa expects the October meeting to centre on the BOJ’s assessment of underlying inflation, with evidence of entrenched wage and price gains, and any signs of an overshoot, deciding the timing and pace of future hikes.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: MUFG says firmer China growth offers yuan support, but uneven demand limits the upside
item.description:
MUFG’s view points to a modestly more supportive backdrop for the yuan, with firmer growth easing pressure on Beijing to add stimulus that could weaken the currency. The caveat is that a recovery led by factories and exports, rather than households, leaves China reliant on external demand and exposed to trade friction, which caps how far that support can run. Monetary policy is the other swing factor: the PBOC’s move to daily overnight funding operations this week has raised questions about whether a lower policy anchor could follow, which would weigh on the yuan if confirmed. For the Australian and New Zealand dollars, firmer industrial output is a mild positive for commodity demand, though a 20% slide in property investment remains a drag on construction materials. For oil, steadier factory activity in the world’s largest crude importer offers some support on the demand side.

-China’s factories have handed the yuan a firmer floor, but MUFG’s warning is that a recovery without the consumer is a recovery built on one leg.

Summary:

  • MUFG says firmer Chinese activity in the third quarter provides a more supportive domestic backdrop for the yuan.
  • The bank cautions that the composition of growth is key to judging whether that support can last.
  • Q3 GDP growth rose to 4.5% from 4.3%, slightly above forecasts, with industrial production accelerating to 5.5% in September.
  • Retail sales improved to 1.1%, helped by the timing of the Mid-Autumn Festival, but household demand has yet to recover convincingly.
  • Property investment fell around 21% in the first three quarters, deepening from the decline through August.
  • Technology manufacturing and digital services continue to outperform traditional domestic sectors.

China’s stronger third-quarter growth gives the yuan a firmer domestic footing, according to MUFG, although the bank cautions that the uneven make-up of the recovery will determine whether that support can be sustained.

MUFG said improving activity, led by industrial production, offers a more supportive backdrop for the currency. However, it noted that stronger output has not yet translated into a convincing recovery in household spending or property investment, making the composition of growth central to the outlook for the yuan.

The data released on Monday showed GDP growth picked up to 4.5% from a year earlier, from 4.3% in the second quarter and slightly ahead of expectations, leaving growth for the year so far at 4.6% and keeping Beijing’s annual target within reach. Industrial production accelerated to 5.5% in September, while the monthly decline in fixed asset investment narrowed after four straight months of double-digit falls.

Consumer demand improved, but with help from the calendar. Retail sales growth rose to 1.1% from 0.4%, well above forecasts, partly because the Mid-Autumn Festival fell in September this year. Property remains the weakest link, with investment down around 21% in the first three quarters, a steeper decline than through August.

MUFG also pointed to a growing divergence within the economy. Technology manufacturing and digital services continued to outperform, while traditional domestic sectors such as property lagged behind.

That divergence matters for the currency. A recovery driven mainly by factories and exports leaves China more dependent on overseas demand and more exposed to trade tensions, while a broader pick-up in household spending would offer a more durable foundation. For now, firmer growth reduces pressure on policymakers to add aggressive stimulus, which tends to support the yuan.

Monetary policy remains an important consideration. The People’s Bank of China said this week it will run daily overnight funding operations through 2 November, a day after Governor Pan Gongsheng flagged plans to study making the overnight rate the central bank’s main policy rate. If that shift eventually brings a lower policy anchor, it could offset some of the support from stronger growth.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: PBOC to run daily overnight reverse repos to Nov 2 in first step after policy rate signal
item.description:
The direct effect should be calmer overnight funding in China’s interbank market through month-end, with the 1 trillion yuan daily cap large enough to stop short-term rates spiking. The bigger market question is the rate the operations carry, which has not been confirmed. If it is set near the current overnight market level of around 1.25%, below the seven-day policy rate of 1.40%, traders may read it as a preview of a lower policy anchor, which would tend to support Chinese government bonds and could weigh on the yuan. If it is set at the top of the existing corridor, it would mainly act as a ceiling and carry little policy signal. For the Australian and New Zealand dollars and for oil, the operations matter only if they turn out to be the first step toward genuine easing that lifts Chinese demand.

---

A day after saying it would study an overnight policy rate, China’s central bank has started using one every day, but until it reveals the price, markets cannot tell whether this is a dress rehearsal or a month-end safety net.

Summary:

  • The People’s Bank of China will conduct overnight reverse repo operations daily from 21 October to 2 November.
  • The operations will use fixed-rate, quantity-based tenders, capped at 1 trillion yuan a day.
  • Foreign-invested banks that act as RMB settlement banks will be eligible counterparties.
  • The move follows Governor Pan Gongsheng’s comments on Monday that the PBOC will study making the overnight rate its main policy rate.
  • The rate for the operations has not yet been confirmed and will be the key signal for markets.
  • It is unclear whether the operations will continue beyond 2 November or are mainly aimed at smoothing month-end liquidity.

China’s central bank will carry out overnight reverse repo operations every day from 21 October to 2 November, putting its newest liquidity tool into regular use a day after Governor Pan Gongsheng said the PBOC would study making the overnight rate its main policy rate.

The People’s Bank of China said the operations will be conducted through fixed-rate, quantity-based tenders, with a cap of 1 trillion yuan a day. In that format, the central bank sets the interest rate and banks bid for the amount of funding they want at that rate. Foreign-invested banks that act as yuan settlement banks will also be eligible to take part.

A reverse repo is a short-term loan from the central bank to commercial banks, secured against bonds. The PBOC currently uses its seven-day reverse repo rate, at 1.40%, as its main policy rate. It introduced overnight operations in June, priced in a corridor around the seven-day rate, but has used them only occasionally until now.

Speaking at the Financial Street Forum in Beijing on Monday, Pan said the overnight interbank rate had effectively already become the central bank’s target and that switching policy operations to an overnight tenor would make interest rate control more precise. He also announced wider access to central bank funding for foreign bank subsidiaries, a theme echoed in Tuesday’s decision to include foreign-invested settlement banks.

Several important details are not yet known. The most significant is the rate. If the operations are priced at the top of the existing corridor, they would act mainly as a ceiling on overnight funding costs. If they are priced closer to the current overnight market rate of around 1.25%, markets may see them as an early test of a lower policy anchor.

It is also unclear whether the daily operations will continue after 2 November. A fixed window could mean the move is mainly about smoothing liquidity over month-end, when Chinese money markets can tighten. An extension would point more clearly toward a permanent shift. The PBOC has not said whether the overnight operations will run alongside its seven-day operations or gradually replace them, and take-up by banks will show how much demand there is for the new facility.

The rate announced with the first operation on Wednesday, and any guidance on what happens after 2 November, will offer the clearest signals yet on how quickly the PBOC intends to move to an overnight policy rate.

item.title: Are US Treasuries still a hedge? Citi Australia CEO says the bonds are losing their edge
item.description:
If more investors share Woodruff’s view, demand for longer-dated Treasuries as portfolio insurance could weaken, adding upward pressure on the term premium, the extra yield investors demand to hold long-term bonds. That would leave yields more exposed to supply and inflation news. It could also support alternatives that investors have been using as hedges, including commodities. Goldman Sachs has said oil is attracting demand as a portfolio hedge, and it sees central bank buying as structural support for gold. Energy is central to the inflation story: higher oil prices linked to the Iran war helped push the US 10-year yield to its highest since 2007 in September, so any renewed spike in crude would reinforce the case that bonds are a weaker shield. The opposing view, from BlackRock, is that today’s higher yields offer more protection than in years.

---

A 5% Treasury yield used to be the perfect insurance policy for a stock portfolio, but Citi’s Australia chief argues inflation and heavy borrowing have made the policy less reliable, and not everyone on Wall Street agrees.

Summary:

  • Citi Australia CEO Mark Woodruff says rising bond supply, persistent inflation and higher neutral interest rates are reducing the appeal of US Treasuries as a portfolio hedge.
  • He said a 5% 10-year yield would usually make Treasuries an ideal hedge for equities, but higher prices and rates have weakened demand.
  • Speaking at Citi’s Australia and New Zealand investment conference in Sydney, he said demand for hedging products has risen, but this cycle is different.
  • The US 10-year yield hit its highest since 2007 in September as rising energy costs pushed inflation higher.
  • Some investors are turning to alternatives such as hedge funds, credit and commodities as stocks and bonds have moved more closely together.
  • BlackRock takes the opposite view, having upgraded Treasuries on the grounds that higher yields offer a bigger cushion.

US Treasuries are becoming less effective as a hedge against falling stock prices, according to Citi Australia Chief Executive Mark Woodruff, who said rising government bond supply, sticky inflation and higher neutral interest rates are undermining their traditional role in portfolios.

Speaking to reporters on Tuesday on the sidelines of Citi’s Australia and New Zealand investment conference in Sydney, Woodruff said a 10-year Treasury yield of around 5% would normally make bonds an ideal hedge for equity holdings. But rising consumer prices and interest rates have weakened demand, he said. While interest in hedging products has increased, he said this cycle is different.

Woodruff pointed to three challenges for the bond market. Supply is rising as governments borrow more. Inflation has remained elevated. And neutral interest rates, the level at which policy neither stimulates nor restrains the economy, have moved higher at central banks around the world. Together, he said, those forces make bonds a less effective hedge than in previous cycles. He added that it is important to keep inflation expectations from becoming embedded.

The comments reflect a broader rethink about the role of government bonds. A hedge works best when it rises in value as stocks fall, but in recent years stocks and bonds have increasingly moved together, particularly when inflation is the main worry. That has led some investors to consider alternatives including hedge funds, credit products and commodities.

The backdrop explains the concern. The US 10-year yield reached its highest level since 2007 in September as global bond markets came under heavy pressure, partly because higher energy costs pushed up inflation. Goldman Sachs made a similar point this week, saying higher starting yields have made bonds a genuine source of return again but not always a reliable hedge for equities. Goldman has also noted that oil is attracting demand as a portfolio hedge.

Not everyone agrees. BlackRock upgraded US Treasuries last week, arguing that higher starting yields provide a bigger cushion against further rate increases and that markets may be pricing in too much Federal Reserve tightening. Morgan Stanley Investment Management has said yields are rising for the right reasons, reflecting strong growth rather than stress, although it remains underweight bond duration and prefers credit.

The debate is likely to hinge on inflation. If price pressures ease and the Fed’s tightening cycle ends, Treasuries could regain their defensive appeal. If inflation stays high, particularly with energy costs elevated by the Iran war, investors may continue to look elsewhere for protection. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

Morgan Stanley thinks the market is underrating Amazon’s cloud business, and with 2 million Nvidia chips on the way, it sees AWS doing the heavy lifting for the next leg higher.

Summary:

  • Morgan Stanley named Amazon a top pick and raised its price target to $350 from $335, keeping an Overweight rating; shares rose as much as 5% on Monday.
  • The bank now expects AWS revenue growth of 47% in 2027 and 42% in 2028, up from 41% and 37%, after Nvidia said AWS is expected to deploy about 2 million of its GPUs over those years.

Morgan Stanley has named Amazon a top pick and raised its price target on the stock to $350 from $335, setting out five catalysts it says could drive shares higher. The stock rose as much as 5% on Monday following the call.

Analyst Brian Nowak, who kept an Overweight rating, said in a note on Sunday that the catalysts could help Amazon stand out in a market where AI leaders and laggards have been changing places. Morgan Stanley sees a bear case of $220 a share and a bull case of $410, which it describes as a risk-reward ratio of about 3 to 1.

The most important driver is Amazon Web Services, the company’s cloud computing unit. Morgan Stanley now expects AWS revenue to grow 47% in 2027 and 42% in 2028, up from earlier forecasts of 41% and 37%. The upgrade follows Nvidia’s disclosure that it expects AWS to buy and deploy about 2 million of its GPUs over those two years. Nowak said he believes AWS’s growth and profit runway remains under-appreciated by the market.

The extra chips come at a cost. Morgan Stanley raised its forecasts for Amazon’s capital spending to $355 billion in 2027 and $365 billion in 2028, underscoring the scale of investment behind the growth story.

The bank also expects AWS profitability to improve, forecasting operating margins of 42% in 2027 and 44% in 2028, which it says would support Amazon earnings of about $16.50 a share in 2028. Its $350 target is based on about 21 times that estimate.

The remaining catalysts extend beyond the cloud. Morgan Stanley said greater visibility into Bedrock, Amazon’s service for accessing AI models, could lift the stock’s valuation from around 15 times 2028 earnings. It also expects Amazon to emerge as a winner as AI shopping agents become more common, potentially through a partnership with Meta’s Muse AI agent over time, with the holiday season the first major test.

Robotics is the fifth catalyst, which Morgan Stanley sees playing out in 2027. The bank estimates that every 10% of Amazon’s global units moved through its robotics-enabled fulfilment centres could save $2 billion to $4 billion a year, and Nowak said efficiency gains appear to be running faster than the bank originally modelled.

The call comes as investors have become more selective within technology, favouring large, well-funded cloud providers over more highly leveraged parts of the AI buildout. Amazon reports its third-quarter results on 29 October after the US market close.

item.title: China holds loan prime rates for 17th month as policy focus shifts to short-term rates
item.description:
The hold was widely expected and should have little direct market impact. The more important signals for traders now come from China’s short-term rates. Monday’s comments from PBOC Governor Pan Gongsheng about moving to an overnight policy rate matter more for the outlook, since the level at which any new rate is set will shape expectations for future easing. With Q3 growth back inside Beijing’s target range and the Federal Reserve tightening, the case for imminent cuts is weak, which limits downside pressure on the yuan from rate differentials. For the Australian and New Zealand dollars and for oil, an unchanged LPR offers no fresh stimulus signal for Chinese demand, keeping the focus on fiscal support and incoming activity data.

Newswire cut: China kept its one-year loan prime rate at 3.0% and five-year at 3.5%, the 17th straight month on hold. The seven-day reverse repo at 1.40% is the main policy rate, and Pan has flagged a move to an overnight rate, but the LPR still prices most loans.

One-line wrap: China’s lending benchmarks have not moved in 17 months, and with the central bank now steering through short-term rates, the LPR has become less a policy lever than a price tag on the country’s loans.

Summary:

  • China left its one-year loan prime rate at 3.0% and its five-year LPR at 3.5% on Tuesday, matching expectations.
  • It is the 17th consecutive month without a change; both rates were last cut in May 2025.
  • The PBOC’s seven-day reverse repo rate, at 1.40%, has been the main policy rate since 2024, with the LPR following its lead rather than acting as a lever in its own right.
  • The LPR remains important as the reference rate for most bank loans, with the five-year tenor guiding mortgage pricing.
  • PBOC Governor Pan Gongsheng said on Monday the central bank will study switching to an overnight policy rate and will allow larger firms to price loans off it instead of the LPR.
  • Q3 GDP growth of 4.5%, above forecasts, has eased pressure for further easing.

China left its benchmark lending rates unchanged for a 17th consecutive month on Tuesday, as expected, with the one-year loan prime rate held at 3.0% and the five-year LPR at 3.5%.

The decision comes as the LPR’s role in Chinese monetary policy continues to shrink. Since a framework change in 2024, the People’s Bank of China has used its seven-day reverse repo rate, currently 1.40%, as its main policy rate. That is the rate the central bank sets directly to steer borrowing costs, and the LPR has followed its lead. With the seven-day rate unchanged, there was little reason for the benchmarks to move.

The LPR has nonetheless kept an important job. It is compiled monthly from quotes submitted by a panel of 20 banks and serves as the reference rate for pricing most new and outstanding loans across the economy. The one-year rate anchors most corporate and household lending, while the five-year rate is the benchmark for mortgages. For borrowers, the LPR remains the number that most directly determines what they pay, even if it no longer drives policy.

That role is set to narrow further. Speaking at the Financial Street Forum in Beijing on Monday, PBOC Governor Pan Gongsheng said the central bank would study switching its main policy operations to an overnight tenor when the time is right, making the overnight reverse repo rate the main policy rate. He also said financially strong companies would be able to choose either the overnight rate or the LPR as the benchmark for floating-rate loans, while lending to households and smaller firms would remain mainly tied to the LPR. The central bank also plans to improve how LPR quotes are set.

Economic conditions also argued against a cut. China’s economy grew 4.5% from a year earlier in the third quarter, slightly above forecasts and back at the bottom of Beijing’s growth target range, with retail sales and industrial output also beating expectations. Abroad, the Federal Reserve’s tightening has kept the gap between US and Chinese bond yields wide, adding to pressure on the yuan if Beijing were to ease. A Reuters poll conducted before the GDP release found economists expect the LPRs and the reserve requirement ratio to stay unchanged through the first quarter of 2027.

Both LPRs were last cut in May 2025, by 10 basis points each. Attention now shifts to the timing of the overnight rate switch and the level at which the new policy rate is set, which will offer a clearer signal of the PBOC’s next move than the monthly LPR fixing.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: PBOC is expected to set the USD/CNY reference rate at 6.6813 – Reuters estimate
item.description:
The fixing mechanism matters most right now because its message has shifted over the past month. For nearly a year, the PBOC has set its daily guidance weaker than market expectations, which traders read as an effort to slow the yuan's appreciation, and in late August that gap reached its widest since February, shortly after the yuan touched a three-and-a-half-year high. Through September, however, the midpoint has strengthened at a faster pace, narrowing its gap with market expectations and suggesting the central bank has eased its resistance to yuan gains. The fixing is still set weaker than models imply, so this looks like a loosening of the brakes rather than their removal. The balance Beijing is weighing is unchanged: a firmer currency supports capital stability and import costs, but too rapid a rise risks eroding export competitiveness while the domestic economy remains soft. The gap between each day's fixing and consensus estimates remains one of the clearest guides to how far the PBOC is willing to let the yuan run.--- The daily fixing is Beijing's quietest but clearest tool for telling markets how fast it wants the yuan to move, and after months of saying slow down, it has lately been saying go, gradually.Summary:
  • The PBOC sets the daily USD/CNY reference rate, or midpoint, at around 0115 GMT, one of the most closely watched signals in Asian FX markets. 
  • China operates a managed floating exchange rate system, allowing the yuan to trade within a band of plus or minus 2% around the daily midpoint during onshore hours. 
  • The midpoint reflects a mix of inputs, including the prior day's close, moves in major currencies, broader international FX conditions and domestic factors such as capital flows and growth momentum, with policymakers retaining discretion over the final number. 
  • If market pressure pushes the yuan toward either edge of the band, the PBOC can intervene through direct buying or selling of yuan, liquidity adjustments, or guidance via state-owned banks. 
  • A stronger-than-expected fixing typically signals the PBOC is leaning against depreciation, while a weaker fixing can indicate tolerance for a softer currency or discomfort with the pace of gains. 
  • For nearly a year the fixing has been set weaker than market estimates, with the gap reaching its widest since February in late August. 
  • In September the PBOC strengthened the fixing for eight straight sessions, the longest run since 2023, and the midpoint reached its strongest level since February 2023. 
  • The yuan has pushed to its strongest levels since early 2023 onshore and since mid-2022 offshore, with Goldman Sachs expecting Beijing to remain comfortable with sustained but gradual appreciation. 
The People's Bank of China sets the daily USD/CNY reference rate at around 0115 GMT, a fixing that remains one of the most closely watched signals in Asian foreign exchange markets. It has taken on added significance in recent weeks as policymakers have shifted from restraining the yuan's rise to guiding it higher.China operates a managed floating exchange rate system, under which the yuan is allowed to trade within a band of plus or minus 2% around the central midpoint set each trading day. That midpoint reflects a mix of inputs, including the previous day's closing price, movements in major currencies such as the US dollar, broader international FX conditions, and domestic considerations like capital flows, growth momentum and financial stability objectives. The calculation is not purely mechanical, giving policymakers room to use the fixing to guide market expectations.Once the midpoint is set, onshore USD/CNY trades freely within the allowable range. Should market pressure push the currency toward either edge of that band, the central bank can step in to smooth volatility, whether through direct buying or selling of yuan, adjustments to liquidity conditions, or guidance channelled through state-owned banks. As a result, the daily fixing is often read as a policy signal rather than a purely technical reference point. A stronger-than-expected midpoint typically suggests the PBOC is leaning against depreciation, while a weaker fixing can signal tolerance for a softer currency, or unease with how quickly the yuan is rising.That second reading has dominated for much of the past year. For nearly a year, the central bank set its daily guidance weaker than market expectations, a pattern traders and analysts interpreted as an attempt to slow the yuan's appreciation. The gap reached its widest since February in late August, shortly after the yuan touched a three-and-a-half-year high against the dollar.September has brought a clear change of tone. The midpoint has strengthened at a faster pace this month, narrowing its gap with market expectations and suggesting the PBOC has eased its resistance to yuan gains. The central bank strengthened the fixing for eight consecutive sessions, the longest streak since 2023, and the midpoint has since reached its strongest level since February 2023. The onshore yuan has traded at its strongest since January 2023, while the offshore rate has reached levels last seen in July 2022. Even so, the fixing is still being set well weaker than market estimates, with one recent midpoint more than 500 pips below a Reuters survey forecast, a reminder that Beijing is allowing appreciation on its own terms rather than stepping aside.The timing has been linked to diplomacy. The underlying tension is a familiar one. A firmer yuan supports capital stability and eases import costs, but a rapid rise risks undermining export competitiveness at a moment when China's broader economy continues to show signs of softness. For traders and investors, the gap between each day's fixing and consensus estimates remains one of the clearest windows into how Beijing is weighing that trade-off, and whether the recent green light for gains stays in place once the summit has passed.

item.title: The Hormuz shipping attacks nobody is counting: inside the US Navy’s go-dark guidance
item.description:
Hormuz attack counts are a floor, and a US Navy FAQ may help explain why

The official tally of attacks on shipping in the Strait of Hormuz is incomplete, and the body that compiles it says so. In its weekly overview on 16 October, the UK Maritime Trade Operations centre (UKMTO) said it was struggling to establish the true number of attacks because the majority of vessels targeted were refusing to report to it. It recorded 12 attacks that week, ten of them inside the Strait, with one vessel lost. It added that it knew of further incidents through other sources but could not include them without verification.

For oil traders, that matters more than any single weekly figure. Freight rates, war-risk premiums and assessments of supply risk all lean on these counts. If most attacked ships are staying silent, the published number is a minimum, not a measure.

Why ships might stay silent

Shipowners have obvious commercial reasons to keep quiet, including insurance complications, exposure with their flag state and sensitivity about routing. But a less noticed document may also be part of the picture.

A US Navy FAQ for shipping companies, highlighted in a post on X by the account @angertab, sets out how the Navy supports transits on the southern route through the Strait. It was issued by the Naval Cooperation and Guidance for Shipping (NCAGS) cell at US Naval Forces Central Command (NAVCENT), the unit that liaises with merchant ships. Copies are posted on the website of the Liberian ship registry and on that of a Turkish shipowners’ and agents’ association.

The FAQ makes clear how limited that support is:

  • What the US provides: airborne overwatch, intelligence and surveillance, and threat response, plus recommended waypoints and transit windows.
  • What it does not provide: no US or partner vessels escort the ships, and no personnel board them.
  • What ships are asked to do: turn AIS tracking off, keep radar on standby and stay silent on VHF radio, because emissions could be used for targeting.
  • On reporting: asked whether the US would give operational security guidance covering crew phones, social media and reporting restrictions, the Navy says best practices will be recommended. It does not say what they are.
  • After the transit: the FAQ says no post-transit debrief is required.

That combination is the point. A ship told to go dark during the transit, and not asked to report afterwards, has little procedural push to file an incident report with UKMTO.

The FAQ does not tell ships to stop reporting attacks. The “reporting restrictions” reference sits in a question about phones and social media, and could simply mean not broadcasting positions online. The document explains how silence could become the default. It does not prove that silence is policy.

A corridor that looks less safe than advertised

The FAQ also contains a reassurance that has aged badly. It says more than 200 transits had been completed with fewer than five successful attacks and no loss of life or vessels. According to the post, the file’s metadata dates it to 14 June, which is before Iran reimposed its blockade in mid-July.

The picture since then is very different. Reported UKMTO data shows that most projectile strikes since early July have hit the southern route, the corridor the US facilitates. October has brought the highest attack totals since the war began on 28 February. If that pattern is confirmed, the route offered as the safer option has become the main target zone, while the reporting that would show it is thinning out.

The post also says the file’s metadata points to an allied, non-US naval connection, suggesting the guidance passed through partner hands. investingLive has not verified this, and at most it shows who handled the file, not who wrote it.

What to watch next

  • UKMTO’s next weekly overview: whether the share of unreported attacks grows, and whether it breaks down incidents by route.
  • NAVCENT or NCAGS: any clarification of what “reporting restrictions” covers, or any updated guidance replacing the June figures.
  • Insurance signals: war-risk premiums and any change to terms for southern-route transits, which would show whether underwriters are pricing in the undercount.
  • Tracked transits: gaps between AIS-visible traffic and US-stated transit figures, which already diverge because facilitated ships run dark.

Practical takeaway: treat weekly Hormuz attack counts as a lower bound. When judging risk to Gulf supply, the direction of the numbers is more reliable than their level, and a quiet week in the data may not be a quiet week at sea.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: JPMorgan brings JPM Coin to Ethereum mainnet: what changes, and what it means for ETH
item.description:
JPMorgan Chase has extended JPM Coin (ticker JPMD), its US dollar deposit token, to the Ethereum mainnet. Approved institutional clients now have a second public network for moving dollars around the clock. Bloomberg reported the move on Monday, 19 October, citing the bank, and the Ethereum Foundation flagged it the same day. JPMD has run on Base, Coinbase’s Ethereum layer-2 network, since November 2025, and Base remains in service.

The move is a meaningful step for Ethereum as financial infrastructure. It is not, on current evidence, a new source of demand for ether. JPMD also remains closed to everyone except approved JPMorgan clients.

What JPM Coin actually is

JPMD is a deposit token: each unit represents one US dollar that a client holds at JPMorgan. That makes it different from a stablecoin such as USDC, which is issued by a non-bank company and backed by reserves held elsewhere. A deposit token is a claim on the bank itself. In effect, it is ordinary commercial bank money moved onto a blockchain.

The practical gain is timing. A transfer that would normally wait on banking hours and business-day settlement can complete almost instantly, at any hour, including weekends.

Why mainnet, when Base was cheaper

Base was promoted on sub-cent fees, and transactions on Ethereum mainnet typically cost more. So the move is not about saving money.

Kinexys, JPMorgan’s blockchain unit, said it chose Ethereum because so much liquidity and so many tokenized assets already sit there. That includes JPMorgan’s own products. The bank launched a tokenized money market fund on Ethereum in December 2025, seeded with $100 million of its own capital. With the cash token and the tokenized securities on the same network, a fund trade and its payment can settle together, without hopping between chains. The bank has also pointed to collateral and tokenized-asset settlement as uses, not just payments.

My read is that this is about settling where the assets already live. Fees are a secondary consideration.

What it does not mean for ETH

JPMD is not ether. Every mainnet transaction pays a fee in ETH, so more institutional activity adds to network usage at the margin. But JPMorgan has not disclosed how much JPMD exists on Ethereum, its contract address, which clients are using it, or how much activity it expects to move from Base.

Without those numbers, there is no basis for treating the launch as a buying catalyst for ETH. It is adoption of the network, not purchases of the coin. It also says nothing about whether JPMorgan holds ether.

What could change the interpretation

The deciding factor is volume. Kinexys is still a small part of a bank whose payments business moves roughly $12 trillion a day.

  • If the supply and activity become public and grow, the story shifts from symbolic to structural.
  • If mainnet usage stays thin, or most activity stays on Base, the launch looks more like positioning than a change in how JPMorgan moves money.

There is also a third venue. JPMorgan is separately working on a phased integration of JPM Coin with Canton Network, a privacy-focused blockchain built for financial markets. That plan was announced earlier this year and has no completed launch date. If activity shifts there, it would suggest the public mainnet is more of a showcase than the main route.

What to watch next

  • Usage data: any JPMorgan disclosure of JPMD supply or volume on mainnet, or a published contract address that lets readers track activity on-chain.
  • Settlement in practice: whether JPMD is used to settle the bank’s tokenized funds on Ethereum, which would confirm the logic behind the move.
  • Canton progress: any concrete launch date for the integration.
  • Rival banks: whether competitors move their deposit-token systems from private ledgers onto public networks.

Practical takeaway: for ETH investors, the useful signal will be usage, not the announcement. Wait for activity you can verify on-chain before treating this as a bullish development for ether. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: BlackRock says French bond sell-off is a lesson in selectivity, upgrades US Treasuries
item.description:
BlackRock’s view reinforces a theme running through bank research this week: higher yields are now the norm, but the reasons behind them matter more than the level. For euro area bonds, the near-term focus is Moody’s decision on France’s credit rating, with a downgrade likely to pressure French debt and widen the gap over German Bunds. Any spillover selling in markets such as Spain could prove an opportunity if fundamentals hold up, in BlackRock’s view. Its upgrade of US Treasuries signals that the world’s largest asset manager sees value in longer-dated US debt at current yields, which could help cap further rises if other investors follow. A rising term premium driven by fiscal worries remains the main risk that could push yields higher still. Elevated energy costs linked to the Iran war add to inflation risks that feed into that premium.

---

Higher yields are everywhere, but BlackRock’s message is that not all of them are worth having, and France shows the difference between being paid more and being paid enough.

Summary:

  • BlackRock says the sharp sell-off in French government bonds shows why investors need to understand what is driving yields higher.
  • France’s 10-year yield has risen about 100 basis points since early August to nearly 5%, with a widening spread over German Bunds reflecting fiscal and political risk.
  • BlackRock sees today’s backdrop as materially different from the 2011-12 euro debt crisis, with stronger banks, more powerful ECB tools and euro area debt back at around 89% of GDP.
  • The firm upgraded US Treasuries last week, trimmed its underweight on Japanese government bonds and favours emerging market local-currency debt, especially in Latin America.
  • In corporate credit, it prefers higher-rated high-yield bonds and avoids both investment grade, under pressure from heavy AI-related issuance, and the weakest borrowers.
  • Markets are watching Moody’s decision on France’s credit rating and UK CPI data this week.

France’s government bond sell-off is a reminder that higher yields are not all equal, according to BlackRock, which says investors need to be increasingly selective as competition for capital intensifies.

BlackRock is the world’s largest asset manager and the owner of iShares, the biggest provider of exchange-traded funds. Its views are closely watched because changes in its asset allocation can influence flows across global markets, and its weekly research from the BlackRock Investment Institute is widely followed as a guide to how big institutional money is positioning.

In its latest commentary, BlackRock said rising government borrowing and AI-related investment are pushing up financing costs globally, exposing borrowers with weakening fundamentals to closer scrutiny. France’s 10-year yield has climbed about 100 basis points since early August to nearly 5%. Part of that reflects the broader global reset in interest rates, but BlackRock said the widening gap between French and German yields shows investors are also demanding extra compensation for France’s fiscal and political risks.

The firm sees risks of spillover from France but does not expect a repeat of the 2011-12 euro debt crisis. France’s government debt has risen from roughly 89% of GDP in 2011 to around 119% today, but the euro area’s overall debt ratio is back at about its 2011 level of around 89%. The region also has stronger banks and more powerful European Central Bank tools, though BlackRock noted intervention is not guaranteed. Indiscriminate selling could create opportunities in markets such as Spain, it said, but it remains neutral on euro area government bonds for now.

Higher yields are also creating opportunities. BlackRock said more than 80% of global bonds now yield above 4%, compared with about 6% five years ago. It upgraded US Treasuries last week, saying higher starting yields provide a bigger cushion against further rate increases and that markets may have priced in too much Federal Reserve tightening. It also trimmed its underweight on Japanese government bonds after long-term yields climbed above 3%, and favours emerging market local-currency debt, particularly in Latin America.

In corporate bonds, BlackRock favours higher-rated high-yield debt for income while avoiding both ends of the credit spectrum. Heavy AI-related issuance is weighing on investment-grade bonds, it said, while the weakest borrowers face tougher refinancing conditions.

The firm also pointed to last week’s tech sell-off, when concerns over the pace of AI spending pushed the Nasdaq down nearly 5%. It still favours AI within a neutral stance on US equities.

Attention now turns to Moody’s decision on France’s credit rating (due froday October 23) and to UK inflation data, which BlackRock will watch for a read on global price pressures. It sees a rise in the term premium, particularly if driven by fiscal concerns, as the key risk that could push yields higher.
